6	
7	# Development Patterns
8	
9	## About
10	
11	Recurring dev conventions worth generalizing to future, different work — not
12	a changelog and not a place for one-off fixes. An entry only belongs here if
13	the pattern should apply beyond the change that established it. Most work
14	sessions should add nothing; see the `development-docs` skill
15	(`.claude/skills/development-docs/SKILL.md`) for the judgment process that maintains
16	this file. Every entry cites a concrete source (commit SHA, PR #, or session
17	detail) for traceability.
18	
19	### Split error handling around a git-landing step
20	
21	**Source:** PR #15 (`worktree-git-integration` branch), `src/wakil/cli/main.py`
22	
23	When a command lands on a branch (`prepare_landing`) before doing risked work (e.g. `apply_capture`/`apply_enrichment`), catch the landing call's `GitServiceError` in its own `try` block, separate from the subsequent operation's errors. On any failure in the operation after a successful landing, call `abandon_landing(config, landing)` so the session doesn't sit on the throwaway ingest branch. `enrich` established this shape first (commit `f5a4ed1`); `_run_ingest` originally wrapped `prepare_landing` and `apply_capture` in one combined `try` block, and was split to match `enrich` in commit `a14af48`.
24	
25	The destination has since changed: `abandon_landing`/`land_ingestion` return to the repository's **default branch**, not to whatever branch the shell happened to be on when the command started. That value used to be frozen in `LandingContext.original_branch` and replayed minutes later (unbounded, for MCP's prepare/apply split), which is how `enrich` came to "return to" a stale, unrelated branch — issue #181. `ensure_clean_for_branch` already guarantees a clean tree at prepare time, so the incidental branch carries no information worth preserving.
26	
27	Two exceptions, both cases where returning is the wrong move:
28	
29	- **The commit itself failed** (#171). `git add` may already have succeeded — the common case is a signing prompt timing out between the `add` and the `commit` — so switching away strands staged work on a branch the caller is no longer on. Stay put.
30	- **HEAD drifted** (`BranchDriftError`, #182/#195). Drift means *another process owns this working tree*. Returning would `git switch` out from under it, which is precisely the clobber the drift detection exists to prevent — so the drift case re-raises without returning, while ordinary push/`gh` failures still return.
31	
32	The rule is "return once the work is durable in git and the tree is still ours; stay put otherwise."
33	
34	The stay-put rule is scoped to the *call*, not to the timeout: `land_ingestion` catches `GitError`, so a rejecting `pre-commit` hook or a signing failure stays put too. That is deliberate — the staged work is equally stranded either way — but only a *killed* commit gets the lock cleanup and recovery text below.
35	
36	Because staying put leaves HEAD somewhere the caller didn't put it, the failure message has to *say so* — both callers name the branch and note that changes may be staged there. Silence was survivable when the session was returned to its own branch; it isn't now. Escape that message: `str(exc)` embeds the hand-finish command, whose commit body is model-generated and routinely contains `[[wikilinks]]` that Rich reads as style tags and deletes — printing a command that looks right and isn't.
37	
38	A killed `git commit` also needs cleaning up after. `subprocess.run` SIGKILLs the child, and git holds `.git/index.lock` for the whole commit — including the signing prompt — so the corpse leaves the lock behind and *every* later git write in the repo fails until someone deletes a file by hand. Recovery advice that assumes the repo is still usable is wrong unless you clear that first; see `_recover_from_killed_commit`.
39	
40	Note: as of this writing PR #15 is still an open draft (unmerged into `main`); the `abandon_landing` half of this pattern applies once/if that branch lands.
41	
42	### Run the live eval before treating new SKILL.md guidance as done
43	
44	**Source:** PR #20 (`docs/skill-guidance-for-linked-context` branch), `src/wakil/skills/entity-enrichment/SKILL.md`
45	
46	Adding a new rule to a skill's SKILL.md and a matching `eval.json` scenario for it isn't finished until `uv run pytest -m eval -k <scenario id>` (a real model call, per `docs/adr/0004`) actually passes — prose that reads correct to a human reviewer can still be misapplied by the model in a way only a live run surfaces. Here, a new rule said an explicit `@file:` reference should be treated as "high-confidence" for back-linking; the model read that confidence as also covering content-worthiness and appended a Timeline entry for a mention the source said had nothing new to report, failing the eval's rubric. The fix was one clarifying sentence separating the link decision from the content decision — but the gap was invisible without actually running the eval. When adding or editing skill guidance, write (or extend) its `eval.json` scenario and run it live before considering the change done, not just at merge/CI time.
47	
48	### A skill's `references/*.md` files are never loaded into the model's context
49	
50	**Source:** `fix/eval-suite-flakiness-and-skill-gaps` branch, live-eval triage session, 2026-07-21
51	
52	`load_skill()` (`src/wakil/llm/skill_loader.py`) builds `skill.body` from `SKILL.md` alone — nothing inlines a skill's `references/*.md` files, even though several SKILL.md files (`source-ingestion`, `skill-authoring`) point at them for what reads as load-bearing judgment ("see `references/source-types.md` for the per-source-type judgment"). This is true both in `wakil enrich`'s real pipeline (`build_system_prompt`) and the eval harness (`run_scenario`) — a human reading the skill file would follow the pointer and find the guidance; the model never does, regardless of how clearly SKILL.md cites the file. Two separate live-eval failures (a fabricated YouTube-transcription workaround, a promotion checklist the model never applied) traced to this exact cause. When a SKILL.md cites a `references/` file for guidance that actually needs to affect model behavior (not just serve as a longer human-readable writeup), pull the load-bearing part into `SKILL.md`'s own body — `references/` can still carry the fuller version, but the file itself must not be the only place the instruction lives.
53	
54	### Check whether a skill's own procedure step order can produce the bug it's trying to prevent
55	
56	**Source:** `fix/eval-suite-flakiness-and-skill-gaps` branch, `note-routing/SKILL.md`, 2026-07-21
57	
58	`note-routing`'s decision tree had "generate the filename" as Step 5 and "surface ambiguity, don't pick" as Step 6 — so a model following the numbered steps in order committed to a filename before ever reaching the ambiguity check the later step was supposed to gate. The instruction to "surface ambiguity" was correct in isolation; the bug was purely in where it sat relative to the step it needed to precede. When a skill's procedure is a numbered sequence and a later step is meant to be a conditional gate on an earlier one, check that the gate actually comes first — a correct rule stated too late in the list doesn't prevent the thing it names.
59	
60	### Print diagnostic detail as it happens, not deferred to a final summary
61	
62	**Source:** `fix/eval-suite-flakiness-and-skill-gaps` branch, `scripts/classify_eval_failures.py` and `uv run pytest -m eval -v` runs, 2026-07-21/22
63	
64	Two separate long-running eval scripts in this session lost their most important output to the same mistake: accumulating results in memory and only printing the useful summary (pytest's failure list, this script's per-item failure reasons) at the very end of the run. `scripts/classify_eval_failures.py` hit a live-model API usage cap partway through a 10-scenario classification pass and crashed — the log had per-scenario pass/fail counts but none of the actual failing rubric items or grader reasons, because those were only assembled into the final `CLASSIFICATION TABLE` the crash never reached. Fixed by printing each individual grading result (pass/fail, failed item, grader reason) immediately as it happens, keeping the end-of-run table as a convenience recap rather than the only place the detail lives. For any script making a sequence of live model calls with real cost/failure risk, print the thing you'd actually need to read *at the point each result arrives*, not after the loop — a partial run should still be a useful run.
65	
66	### Zip a vendored data file, document its source in a sibling `.SOURCE.md`
67	
68	**Source:** PR #21 (`refactor/candidate-notes-stopword-filtering` branch), `src/wakil/app/data/`
69	
70	When vendoring a third-party data file (a word list, a static lookup table) into the repo, zip it rather than committing plain text — `common_words.zip` is 17KB against the original 34KB `common_words.txt`, decompressed once at import time via the stdlib `zipfile` module, not re-read per call. Because a zip's contents aren't reviewable in a plain `git diff`, add a sibling `<name>.SOURCE.md` documenting where the data came from, its license, and how to regenerate/refresh it — `common_words.SOURCE.md` is the template to copy for the next one.
71	
72	### A full live-model eval-suite run has a high baseline failure rate — don't read it as a regression signal
73	
74	**Source:** session comparing `uv run pytest -m eval -q` across PRs #21-#24 and `main`, 2026-07-21
75	
76	Running the complete `-m eval` suite (all skill scenarios, not a single targeted scenario) produced roughly 45-53% failures on every branch tested, including ~16-17 of 47 scenarios that failed identically across branches with zero code overlap (SCHEMA.md removal, capture-time model calls, candidate-filtering, related-notes search — none of which share a code path). Every unique-to-one-branch failure spot-checked was the same character of failure: a subjective "did the model stay strictly within its stated skill boundary" or "did it avoid inventing a disambiguating detail" rubric item, not a functional break. This matches `docs/adr/0004`'s own rationale for excluding these from the required CI gate. Before treating a full-suite eval run's failures as evidence of a regression, compare against a same-day `main` baseline (or re-run the specific failing scenario in isolation) rather than reading the raw failure count at face value — a targeted, single-scenario eval run (e.g. verifying one new rubric item after a SKILL.md wording change) is a much more reliable signal than a full-suite sweep.
77	
78	### An ADR's `status: accepted` means the decision was made, not that it was implemented
79	
80	**Source:** `docs/relationship-graph-traversal-proposal.md`, 2026-07-23
81	
82	ADR 0006 ("Backlinks as a Live Query Over a Widened Relationship Table") is `status: accepted` and its schema/migration exist, but grepping the real application code turned up exactly one place a `Relationship` row is ever constructed (`ingest_service.py`'s `apply_enrichment`) — and it only ever writes `subject_memory_id`/`object_memory_id`. The note-note columns the ADR is about (`subject_note_id`/`object_note_id`) are populated nowhere in the real pipeline, exercised only by one hand-constructed unit test roundtrip. This wasn't caught until a downstream consumer (a kb-side skill assuming backlinks were already automatic) went looking for the actual write path. Before citing an accepted ADR's decision as current, working behavior in a new design doc, a docstring, or downstream documentation, grep for where it's actually implemented — `status: accepted` records that a decision was made, not that every consequence of it landed in code.
83	
84	### Diarized transcript formats each get their own `parse_<x>_transcript()` sharing one merge helper
85	
86	**Source:** `fix/json-transcript-diarization` branch, `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`, 2026-07-25
87	
88	A plain-JSON transcript export (`{"segments": [{"speaker": "Speaker 1", "text": ..., "start": ...}]}`) looked like the same shape as an Apple `.whisper` zip archive's `metadata.json` (`{"transcripts": [{"speaker": {"name": ...}, ...}]}`) but wasn't — different container (zip vs. plain file), different top-level key (`transcripts` vs. `segments`), different speaker shape (object vs. flat string) — so it fell through `prepare_capture`'s generic text branch and captured as a raw, undiarized JSON blob instead of dialogue. The fix factored the actual merge logic (consecutive-same-speaker turns, filler-word stripping) out of `parse_whisper_transcript` into a shared `_dialogue_from_segments(segments, speaker_of)` helper, then added `parse_json_transcript()` as a second, format-specific caller. The next new diarized export shape (a different ASR tool's JSON, an SRT-with-speaker-labels variant, etc.) should follow the same shape: a small `parse_<x>_transcript()` that extracts its own `segments` list and a `speaker_of` callable, gated on file suffix/content in `prepare_capture`, reusing `_dialogue_from_segments` rather than re-implementing the merge.
89	
90	### Anthropic prompt caching needs an identical prefix through `system` too, not just a matching shared block
91	
92	**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** commit 6b64a5a, `src/wakil/llm/client.py`, `ModelClient.complete()`'s `cacheable_prefix` param
93	
94	Marking a block with `cache_control` only produces a cache hit if everything before it in the request — `system` included — is byte-identical to a previous call within the TTL. `build_system_prompt` (`skill_loader.py`) bakes each DAG stage's skill body + JSON schema into `system`, so the extraction/resolution/revision calls in one `wakil enrich` run never share a cache lineage even though they all send the same source document — their `system` differs first, breaking the prefix chain before it ever reaches the shared content. `cacheable_prefix` on `ModelClient.complete()` therefore only pays off *within* one call type (retries, and any future batched sub-calls of the same call), never *across* call types, unless `system` itself is made call-invariant — which has its own cost (skill/schema content would move into the user message, a weaker instruction-following position). Before assuming a shared block will cache across two different call sites, check whether their `system` is actually identical first.
95	
96	### `thinking.budget_tokens` doesn't exist on `claude-opus-4-8` and later — use `output_config.effort` or `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` instead
97	
98	**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0015-relevance-gated-entities-and-truncation-driven-batching.md` (Decision 2, Step A), `src/wakil/llm/client.py`'s `DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`
99	
100	`AnthropicClient.complete` hardcodes `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` with no way to bound how much of `max_tokens` thinking consumes before output starts. The obvious lever — `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` — returns a 400 error on `claude-opus-4-8` (this codebase's `DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`) and every later model in the family (Opus 4.7+, Fable 5, Mythos 5), confirmed against Anthropic's live migration guide (platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/migration-guide.md) and not just assumed. The two levers that are actually available on this model, confirmed against the installed SDK's type stubs (`anthropic` package, `types/output_config_param.py`, `types/thinking_config_disabled_param.py`): `output_config={"effort": "low"|"medium"|"high"|"xhigh"|"max"}` (compatible with adaptive thinking, currently never set — the call runs at whatever server-side default applies), and `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` (eliminates thinking-token cost entirely, at the cost of whatever quality adaptive thinking buys). Before adding a `budget_tokens` cap to any Anthropic call in this codebase, check the current model's actual capability — model-specific thinking/effort support changes across the Claude model lineage, and a docs page is one step removed from observed behavior, so verify with a live call before relying on either lever in production.
101	
102	### An entity-revision candidate's `content` is one shared in-memory value across prompt, merge, and stale-guard — trace all three before changing what it holds
103	
104	**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** ADR 0016 review (rejected "gated context-trimming" design), `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`
105	
106	`_run_entity_updates` reads each candidate's target-note content exactly once into a `content` string (part of the `_EntityCandidate` tuple), and that same in-memory value is reused three separate times downstream: as the model prompt's input (`_revise_candidates`), as the merge's `old_content` (`_apply_entity_revisions`, `by_path.get(...)`), and as the comparison baseline for `apply_enrichment`'s stale-file guard (`update.old_content`, checked against a fresh disk read at apply time). Nothing re-reads the file between prepare and apply. An ADR proposing to trim that string for just the prompt (to cut context cost) initially claimed the merge step was unaffected because it "always re-reads the full file at apply time" — checked against the actual code, it doesn't; the claim was simply wrong, and acting on it would have silently broken the stale-guard (a trimmed string can never match a fresh full read), the merge (no Timeline heading left for `_TIMELINE_HEADING_RE` to find), and `_split_candidates_by_content_length`'s cost-balancing (which sizes candidates by `len(content)`) all at once, for exactly the notes the change was meant to help. Before changing what a shared value like this holds for one consumer, grep for every other place that same variable/field is read, not just the one motivating the change.
107	
108	### Known issue: `_resolve_entity_slug` silently picks a winner on a cross-type slug collision
109	
110	**Source:** PR #33 (`feat/entity-compile-pilot` branch), `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`, session discussion 2026-07-26
111	
112	`_resolve_entity_slug(config, slug)` (backing `wakil entities compile SLUG`) searches every entity type's canonical directory, sorted alphabetically, for a file named `<slug>.md`, and returns the first match — its own docstring says "only one page per slug is expected to exist in practice," but nothing enforces that. If two entities of different types ever share a slug (e.g. a person and a company both slugifying to `edward-bridges`), the resolver silently returns whichever directory sorts first (`companies` before `people`, alphabetically) with no error and no indication a second match exists. The only mitigating factor is that the preview step shows the full resolved path before the user confirms — but nothing actively flags the ambiguity, so an inattentive confirm could compile the wrong entity. Not yet fixed. The intended fix, if picked up: keep the bare-slug ergonomics for the (overwhelmingly common) unambiguous case, but have `_resolve_entity_slug` detect a match in more than one directory and raise a clear error listing every match, directing the user to a full relative path instead of silently guessing — the same "surface ambiguity, don't pick" discipline `note-routing/SKILL.md` already applies to filename generation (see the entry above on step ordering).
113	
114	### Adding a mandatory model call to the enrichment DAG means auditing every `FakeClient(...)` construction, not just bumping a default
115	
116	**Established:** 2026-07-27 · **Source:** issue #70, `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`'s `_synthesize_stub_content`, `tests/unit/test_ingest_service.py`
117	
118	`prepare_enrichment`'s DAG (extraction → entity-resolution → entity-updates → …) is exercised almost entirely through `FakeClient`, a fixed-length scripted-response queue with no notion of "this call is optional" — each test's list length has to exactly match however many real model calls that specific resolution shape triggers. Adding a new *unconditional* call partway through the DAG (here: synthesize content for every create-resolution's stub once it survives suppression) broke every test whose fixture happened to produce that condition, not just the ones that explicitly asserted a call count — including tests using the bare default `FakeClient()` and tests with an explicit 2-3-item list built for the DAG shape *before* the new call existed. There is no shortcut around this: bumping `FakeClient.__init__`'s default queue only covers bare `FakeClient()` callers; every explicit-list construction still has to be individually re-derived (does this resolution's create survive suppression? does an update-candidate's target file exist on disk?) and given one more scripted response, or the test fails opaquely with "FakeClient ran out of scripted responses" rather than a clear diff. When adding a new call to this (or any other) fixed-length-fake-backed DAG, budget time to grep every construction site of the fake client, not just its default, before trusting a green test run.
119	
120	### Stacked same-file refactor PRs from a shared base conflict on sequential merge even when the functions they touch don't overlap
121	
122	**Established:** 2026-07-30 · **Source:** PRs #109, #110, #111 (three independent function-level refactors of `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`, each branched from the same pre-refactor commit)
123	
124	Three worktree-agent PRs each extracted helpers from a *different* function in `ingest_service.py` (`apply_enrichment`, `_build_stub_entities`, `validate_proposal`), with no line ranges in common. Merging the first two into `main` sequentially was a clean fast-forward, but the third (`validate_proposal`) then failed `gh pr merge` with a conflict, because git's diff anchors on the *text* around a change, not on which named function it belongs to — once `apply_enrichment`'s body was replaced by a call to its new helpers on `main`, the region immediately following the still-unrefactored (from that branch's point of view) `validate_proposal` no longer matched what the `validate_proposal` branch expected to find there, even though neither PR touched the other's actual function body. Rebasing the trailing branch onto the new `main` reproduces the same conflict (it's not merge-order-specific); resolving it requires re-deriving the intended final file — start from `main`'s current version of the file and manually re-apply just the extracted-function's diff, rather than trying to hand-resolve `<<<<<<<`/`>>>>>>>` markers in place, since the marked regions don't line up with either branch's actual intended change. When queuing multiple same-file refactor PRs from one audit, expect this on any PR after the first that touches that file, and budget for a manual reconciliation pass rather than a routine merge.
125	
126	### MCP tools live in `mcp/tools.py` as plain functions; `mcp/server.py` wraps them in closures for FastMCP registration
127	
128	**Established:** 2026-07-28 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0018-mcp-interface.md`, `src/wakil/mcp/tools.py`/`server.py`
129	
130	FastMCP's `@mcp.tool()` decorator introspects the wrapped function's signature to build the tool's client-facing JSON schema — any parameter present on that function becomes something the MCP client is expected to supply. Every wakil MCP tool needs a `WorkspaceConfig` (and the write tools need the shared `ProposalCache`) that must stay fixed for the life of one `wakil mcp serve` process, not be re-supplied per call, so those can't be plain parameters on the decorated function. `mcp/tools.py` holds the actual logic as ordinary functions taking `config`/`cache` explicitly first, directly unit-testable with no running server (`tests/unit/test_mcp_tools.py` calls them with no MCP machinery at all); `mcp/server.py`'s `build_server(config)` builds one `ProposalCache`, then registers a thin closure per tool that captures `config`/`cache` and forwards only the remaining, client-facing parameters. The next new MCP tool should follow the same split — logic in `tools.py`, a same-named closure wrapper in `server.py` — rather than writing logic directly inside a `@mcp.tool()`-decorated function.
131	
132	### A `FakeClient`'s strict queue order stops being reliable once two of its calls run on separate threads
133	
134	**Established:** 2026-08-03 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0020-enrich-progress-visibility-concurrency-and-checkpointing.md` (Decision 2), `tests/unit/test_ingest_service.py`'s `FakeClient`
135	
136	`prepare_enrichment`'s DAG nodes 3 and 4 (`_run_entity_updates`/`_synthesize_stub_content`) now run concurrently via a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, and both share the exact same contract (`EntityRevisionOutput`) and system prompt — indistinguishable to a scripted fake except by which one calls `complete()` first, which thread scheduling now decides rather than the DAG's own code order. Any test that scripted both calls into one `FakeClient([...])` queue and asserted something about a *specific* one of them (its prompt content, or a response tailored to one call but not the other) is flaky under this change, even though the test never mentions threads. `FakeClient` gained an optional `router` param — a list of `(prompt-substring, response)` pairs checked before the queue on every `complete()` call — so a test can pin a specific response to whichever call's prompt contains a target note path unique to it (revision targets and synthesis targets never overlap), while leaving the other call to draw from the plain queue. When adding concurrency between two DAG calls that share a contract, grep every existing scripted-fake test that exercises both calls in one run before trusting a green suite — a call-order assumption baked into fixture data doesn't show up as a diff anyone reviews.
137	
138	### A back-compat check must be computed from a frozen copy of the old behavior, never from the current function
139	
140	**Established:** 2026-08-09 · **Source:** PR #194 review rounds 2–3; `_LEGACY_BRACKET_TS_RE` and `PRE_179_MD_HASH` in `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py` / `tests/unit/test_ingest_service.py`
141	
142	When a change alters a stored, derived value — a content hash, a slug, a serialized key — the fallback that recognizes already-stored values has to reproduce *what the old code produced*, which means a frozen copy of the old logic, not a call to the current function. #194 wrote `legacy_text = clean_transcript(raw)` intending "what this hashed to before"; because the same PR had also changed `clean_transcript`'s regex, the fallback was inert for exactly the files it existed for. Two symptoms to watch for: the guard silently never fires, and any test of it passes tautologically because both sides of the comparison move together — pin the literal expected value (a digest, a string) computed against a real pre-change checkout, and say in a comment that it must not be regenerated from `HEAD`. Also enumerate every input path the changed function serves, not just the one in the PR's headline: the same fix initially covered `.md` only, while the regex change affected `.txt`/`.srt` captures identically.
143	
144	### `EnrichmentCheckpoint` persists each `wakil enrich` DAG phase; a crash or failed `validate_proposal` is not always a full redo
145	
146	**Established:** 2026-08-03 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0020-enrich-progress-visibility-concurrency-and-checkpointing.md` (Decision 3), `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`
147	
148	Before assuming a killed/crashed `wakil enrich` run — or one that failed `validate_proposal` for a reason unrelated to any of its 4 model calls — always means starting over: check for `EnrichmentCheckpoint` rows for that source first (`sqlite3 <workspace>/wakil.db 'select phase, created_at from enrichment_checkpoints where source_id = N'`). Each of `prepare_enrichment`'s 4 phases (extraction, resolution, revision, synthesis) is checkpointed on clean completion, keyed by `sha256(source.content_hash | context_digest | model)` — a re-invocation with the same key skips straight past any phase with a matching row. Only clean completions are cached, never a model-call failure (extraction/resolution's `ModelContractError` branches skip the save so a transient failure stays retriable), and only `--force` or a successful `apply_enrichment` ever clears them — a declined preview or a failed `validate_proposal` leaves them in place deliberately. `_build_stub_entities` itself is never checkpointed (only its input, `entity_resolutions`, is) — it always re-runs fresh from whatever resolutions end up on the proposal, so it can't drift between a live and a resumed run.
149	
150	
151	### A tolerant read is for display; a decision needs a checked read
152	
153	**Established:** 2026-08-08 · **Source:** issue #180/#181, the #195 review, `src/wakil/integrations/git.py`'s module docstring
154	
155	`integrations/git.py` deliberately returns `None`/`[]` when a git read fails, so `wakil status` can never crash on a weird repo. That tolerance is right for rendering and wrong for deciding, and the two had been sharing one helper:
156	
157	- `changed_files` failing → `ensure_clean_for_branch` reads "tree is clean" → wakil branches and commits **on top of the user's uncommitted work**.
158	- `branch_exists` failing → `_resume_source_branch` reads "no such branch" → cuts a **second** branch for a source that already had one, and the DB then disagrees with reality permanently.
159	- `resolve_default_branch` failing → `create_branch_from(base=None)` → cuts an "ingest" branch off **whatever unrelated branch is checked out**.
160	
161	Each of those is a silent wrong action produced by a failed read, not by a wrong answer. The fix is a pair per read: keep the tolerant form for display (`changed_files`, `branch_exists`, `resolve_default_branch`, `inspect_git`) and add a checked sibling that raises (`status_lines`, `require_branch_exists`, `require_default_branch`, `current_branch`). Where a non-zero exit is itself a legitimate answer — "no such ref" — use a tri-state probe (`_run_git_probe`) so "absent" and "couldn't run git" stay distinguishable.
162	
163	The generalizable rule: **before using a subprocess-wrapper's return value, ask what it returns when the subprocess fails, and whether that value is safe as an answer.** `None`-on-failure is a fine contract, but it means "no information", and code that treats it as "no" will act. This applies equally to `integrations/github.py` (a `gh` auth failure must not read as "there is no PR") and to any future wrapper of an external binary.
164	
165	### Instants stay UTC; calendar dates are local
166	
167	**Established:** 2026-08-07 · **Source:** issue #174, `workspace_today()` in `src/wakil/config/settings.py`
168	
169	Every user-visible date in wakil used to come from `datetime.now(UTC).date()`. For a single-user local tool that is simply wrong: a capture run at 20:49 US-Eastern is already tomorrow in UTC, so four consecutive evening ingests in one session were all stamped a day ahead of the meetings they recorded — in the auto-generated `title`, in `captured`/`created`, and in the raw file's own date-prefixed filename.
170	
171	The fix draws a line that any new date-producing code needs to stay on the right side of:
172	
173	- **A calendar date a human reads is local.** `created`/`retrieved` frontmatter, the date prefix on a raw capture's filename, Timeline entry headings, and the "today" passed into a prompt. These go through `workspace_today(config)` for "now", or `workspace_date(config, instant)` for a value that is already a timestamp (a `.whisper` archive's `dateCreated`, a `Source.retrieved_at`) — both honour the workspace's optional `timezone:` key and otherwise use the machine's local zone. Never call `.date()` on a UTC-aware datetime to get one of these; that yields the UTC day, which is the whole bug.
174	
175	  Two deliberate exceptions: the `wakil/ingest/<date>-<slug>` branch name is still UTC (`git_service.py`), left alone to avoid conflicting with in-flight work on that file — a branch name is not knowledge-base content. And an authored `captured:`/`date:` value in an input file is the *user's own* date, preserved verbatim rather than converted.
176	- **An instant used for ordering or arithmetic stays UTC.** `storage/schema.py`'s `utcnow()` still backs every `created_at`/`retrieved_at`/`last_seen_at` column. These are timestamps, not dates: `memory_service.retrieval_rank`'s age computation and every `ORDER BY` depend on a single monotonic reference, and making them local would break both across a DST boundary.
177	
178	Two practical consequences worth knowing before writing the next date-touching test or helper. First, `tests/conftest.py` now pins `TZ=UTC` (with `time.tzset()`), because otherwise a test asserting a date in a filename passes in a UTC CI runner and fails on a US-Eastern laptop — pin or freeze the clock rather than asserting today's date directly. Second, `workspace_today` needs a `WorkspaceConfig`, and several enrichment helpers deep in `ingest_service.py` don't have one in scope; those take an explicit `today: str` parameter computed by a caller that does, rather than acquiring a config just to read a date. Prefer that over threading `config` through another layer.
179	
180	### A budget-capped model input must announce the cap in both directions
181	
182	**Established:** 2026-08-07 · **Source:** issue #176, `_truncate_source` in `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`; second instance of the shape recorded at `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`'s "Workspace guide file (RESOLVER.md) is silently truncated at 4,000 chars"
183	
184	`prepare_enrichment` cut its source at `MAX_SOURCE_CHARS` (24,000) with `text[:MAX_SOURCE_CHARS]` and said nothing to anyone. A ~28-minute transcript exceeded that, so the model wrote that a topic "is not present in the captured transcript here" — a *true* statement about the input it received, which the operator read as a false claim about their own recording and filed as a synthesis-accuracy bug. The model was right and the tool was wrong.
185	
186	This is the second recorded instance of the same shape (RESOLVER.md's 4,000-char cut was the first), so it is worth stating as a rule rather than a fix: **any place a budget cap trims model input needs two announcements, not one.**
187	
188	- **Tell the model**, inline in the text it receives, that its view is partial and what it must not conclude from that. A cap that is invisible to the model licenses exactly the reasoning-about-absence that caused this: it cannot distinguish "not in the source" from "not in my slice of the source."
189	- **Tell the operator**, on the proposal/result, with the scale of the loss. "Summary of a 28-minute call seems thin" is not diagnosable; "truncated to 24,000 of 61,400 characters" is.
190	
191	Append the notice rather than substituting it into the budget, and assert in a test that the analyzed prefix is byte-identical to what it was before — otherwise a fix for visibility quietly shrinks the input it was meant to explain.
192	
193	Both recorded instances now go through one helper, `_cut_to_budget(text, cap=…, label=…, unanalyzed=…)`: `MAX_SOURCE_CHARS` on the source (enrichment *and* the capture-metadata call, whose abstract is durable), and `GUIDE_MAX_CHARS` on `RESOLVER.md`. Reach for it rather than writing a third bare slice — a cap that isn't announced is indistinguishable, from the outside, from the model getting the answer wrong.
194	
195	### Adding SKILL.md guidance has a budget cost that can degrade an unrelated step
196	
197	**Established:** 2026-08-07 · **Source:** issue #176, `note-revision/SKILL.md`, four measured live-eval runs
198	
199	Adding three sections and one procedure step to `note-revision/SKILL.md` (197 → 257 lines) made the new pronoun scenario pass and made an **unrelated, pre-existing** scenario fail — `no-existing-note-handoff-to-content-synthesis`, whose failing rubric item is about accurately enumerating the workspace's files during Step 1. Measured, not assumed: 3/3 failures on the edited skill, 1/1 pass on `main`'s version of the same file, same day.
200	
201	Two rounds of tuning followed, and each fixed one failure by causing the other:
202	
203	| variant | lines | pronoun scenario | handoff scenario |
204	|---|---|---|---|
205	| new step + sections mid-file | 257 | pass | **fail** |
206	| compressed prose | 233 | pass | **fail** |
207	| scan folded into an existing step, sections moved to end | 230 | **fail** | pass |
208	| dedicated step restored, sections at end | 231 | pass | (regression stands) |
209	
210	Two things to take from this. First, **a skill's instruction budget is real** — guidance is not free to add, and the cost lands on whichever step is competing for attention, not necessarily on anything topically related to what you added. Budget an eval run for scenarios you did *not* touch, not just the one you wrote. Second, the third row is the same finding already recorded above under "Check whether a skill's own procedure step order can produce the bug it's trying to prevent": demoting the pronoun scan from its own numbered step to a clause inside another step broke it. A gate needs to be a step.
211	
212	Stopping after two rounds was deliberate, per this file's own entry on the personal-reflection heuristic: when each round of tuning trades one failure for another, the approach is the problem, not the tuning. The remaining regression is on a picky file-enumeration rubric item and is documented in the PR rather than tuned against.
213	
214	### An eval must put a production signal in the channel production puts it in
215	
216	**Established:** 2026-08-09 · **Source:** the [#202 review](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/202), `src/wakil/skills/transcript/eval.json`
217	
218	`transcript`'s new truncation scenario pasted the `[SOURCE TRUNCATED: …]` marker into the scenario's `query`. In production, `_truncate_source` appends that marker to the *source text* — the untrusted content channel the model is asked to analyze, at the end of a long document, where it is easy to miss or to mistake for transcript content. `tests/evals/runner.py` renders `query` as the leading instruction and `workspace.overlay` files as pasted content, so the eval was testing the strictly easier case and would have kept passing if the notice had regressed into the source body.
219	
220	The rule generalizes past this one scenario: **an eval scenario's `query` is the operator's instruction, and `workspace.overlay` is everything the tool assembles.** Anything the code puts in the prompt on the operator's behalf — a truncation marker, a schema block, a related-notes digest — belongs in the overlay, positioned where the code positions it. A signal moved into the instruction slot tests instruction-following, not the behaviour under test.
221	
222	### A skill rule keyed on an input the call never receives is a bias, not a constraint
223	
224	**Established:** 2026-08-09 · **Source:** issue #176, PR #202 review rounds 1 and 2 — `note-revision/SKILL.md`, `entity-compile/SKILL.md`, `schema/entities/person.yaml`
225	
226	A rule shaped "use X if the page declares it, otherwise fall back to Y" reads like a constraint and behaves like an unconditional instruction to do Y, whenever X is not actually reachable. The model can't report that its premise was unavailable; it just always takes the else-branch. This shipped twice in one PR, in two different ways:
227	
228	- **No producer.** `note-revision` was told to take pronouns from a `pronouns:`/`gender:` field. Nothing declared that field in any entity schema and nothing ever wrote one, so the rule could only ever resolve to they/them — including on pages where a source had stated the pronouns outright.
229	- **No channel.** `entity-compile` got the same rule, and `prepare_entity_compile` hands that call `post.content` — frontmatter stripped. Even after `person.yaml` declared the field, this call could not see it, so a page reading `pronouns: she/her` would have had its Compiled Truth *rewritten* to they/them. A durable rewrite of correct user content, by a rule added to prevent exactly that.
230	
231	Two checks before adding a rule that reads a field, a section, or a prior value:
232	
233	1. **Trace the producer.** Grep for something that writes it. If nothing does, the rule needs a supply side in the same change, or it is not a rule.
234	2. **Trace the prompt.** Find the `build_*_prompt` for that DAG stage and confirm the value is in what it assembles. `note-revision` gets `current_full_content` (frontmatter included); `entity-compile` gets `entity_name` + two section strings. Two skills, same sentence, different reachability.
235	
236	When the value genuinely isn't available, don't pass it in reflexively — re-scope the rule to what the call *can* check. `entity-compile`'s became "carry forward whatever pronouns the prose already uses; never introduce one," which is satisfiable with its real inputs and happens to sit better with its additive-only doctrine anyway.
237	
238	Note that an eval will not catch this on its own: `tests/evals/runner.py` pastes whole files, frontmatter included, so a scenario written the obvious way passes while production fails. That is the sibling entry above ("An eval must put a production signal in the channel production puts it in"), applied to the input channel — the fix is to put the value where production puts it, which for this case meant carrying the pronouns in the page's prose.
239

1	---
2	title: Relevance-Gated Entity Selection and Truncation-Driven Batching for Entity Revision Calls
3	status: accepted
4	date: 2026-07-25
5	audience: wakil design
6	---
7	
8	# Relevance-Gated Entity Selection and Truncation-Driven Batching for Entity Revision Calls
9	
10	`status: accepted` means the design below is settled. Decision 1 is
11	implemented (pending its live-eval gate, see Consequences). Decision 2 is
12	fully implemented: Step A was tried and ruled out live; Step B (bisection)
13	is implemented, unit-tested, and live-validated against the real
14	originally-failing transcript — see PR #32.
15	
16	## Context
17	
18	The entity-revision DAG node (`_run_entity_updates` in `app/ingest_service.py`,
19	the third model call in ADR 0008's classify/extract/resolve/enforce/finalize
20	decomposition) batches every `action=update` entity-resolution result into a
21	single model call and asks it to decide, per entity, whether the source
22	warrants a real change to that entity's page — and if so, to re-synthesize
23	the page's entire "Compiled Truth" section, not just a diff.
24	
25	A real `wakil enrich` run against a Scorealytics planning-meeting transcript
26	touching 10 already-paged entities failed with a truncated response even
27	after `complete_with_contract`'s existing doubling retry (8192 → 16384
28	tokens) — a recurrence of a previously-documented failure mode
29	(`docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`, "`EOF while parsing a string` ... may mean the
30	model response was truncated," 2026-07-20), whose original fix (detect
31	truncation distinctly, double the budget once) was a stopgap for surfacing
32	the failure clearly, not a structural fix for large batches.
33	
34	Diagnosing this run surfaced two separate, compounding problems:
35	
36	1. **Every existing-page entity a source mentions becomes an equally-weighted
37	   "update" candidate**, regardless of how central it actually is to the
38	   source. `entity-resolve/SKILL.md`'s original wording made this
39	   unconditional ("a page for this entity already exists ... a later step
40	   decides what, if anything, should change"). The resolution step's
41	   `confidence` field looked like it might already capture this, but
42	   checking a real run's output against the user's own relevance
43	   assessment of the same 10 entities showed a clean divergence: a company
44	   mentioned only once, in passing, as background context (the reason for
45	   a scheduling constraint, never itself discussed) scored `confidence:
46	   0.95` — indistinguishable from the meeting's actual participants —
47	   because `confidence` was answering a different question (identity-match
48	   certainty: "is this definitely the same Mosaic as the existing page")
49	   than relevance ("does this source actually concern Mosaic"). Neither
50	   the Pydantic field nor the skill file had ever defined what `confidence`
51	   was supposed to mean; nothing downstream used it beyond CLI display.
52	
53	2. **Batching many candidates into one revision call risks truncation, and
54	   the one failure observed so far doesn't cleanly indict a particular
55	   cause.** Only ~2644 characters (~660 tokens at a 4-chars/token estimate)
56	   of actual output had been generated by the time the 16384-token ceiling
57	   hit — meaning roughly 96% of the consumed budget went to
58	   `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` reasoning, not the text the model was
59	   asked to produce. That rules out "the response text itself is too long"
60	   as the primary story. It does **not**, on its own, establish how thinking
61	   cost scales with what's in the request — with a single data point, "cost
62	   scales with entity count," "cost is a large fixed per-call overhead
63	   independent of count," and "cost scales with something else entirely
64	   (e.g. ambiguity of the has_update judgment)" are all still consistent
65	   with the evidence. Any batching or budget-bounding response to this
66	   failure is, honestly, a hypothesis to be checked against a rerun of the
67	   real failing case — not a conclusion the one incident already proves.
68	
69	## Decision
70	
71	**1. Separate relevance from confidence as two independently-judged fields**
72	(implemented; commit `a656537` on branch
73	`feat/entity-revision-caching-and-relevance`):
74	
75	- `EntityResolution` gains `relevance: central | notable | minor |
76	  peripheral | None`, judged by the resolution step from the same source
77	  read it already performs to decide `create`/`update`/`skip` — no
78	  additional model call. `confidence` gains an explicit field description
79	  constraining it to identity-match certainty, distinct from relevance.
80	  Both are defined with worked examples in `entity-resolve/SKILL.md`.
81	- `_run_entity_updates` excludes `minor`/`peripheral` candidates before the
82	  (expensive) revision call. Missing/`None` relevance is treated as
83	  inclusive by omission — a model that doesn't emit the field never
84	  silently loses an entity that should have been updated.
85	- Excluded entities are surfaced as a visible `proposal.warnings` entry
86	  ("N entities left untouched as below the relevance threshold: ...")
87	  rather than dropped without a trace, and the CLI's entity-resolution
88	  preview table gained a Relevance column alongside the existing
89	  Confidence column — reviewable before anything is applied, per
90	  `CLAUDE.md`'s "show reviewable diffs for knowledge-base modifications"
91	  and "do not silently rewrite user knowledge." This is the same
92	  visibility contract every other degraded-but-non-blocking outcome in
93	  this DAG already uses (a missing target file, a failed resolution call);
94	  it is not a new, weaker pattern introduced here.
95	- **Not yet done, required before Decision 1 is considered complete**: a
96	  live-model eval scenario for `entity-resolve/SKILL.md`'s new relevance
97	  guidance, per this project's own established norm (ADR 0004) that new
98	  judgment guidance — as opposed to deterministic code — needs live
99	  verification, not just schema-level unit tests. The only calibration
100	  this field currently has is the single case study that motivated this
101	  ADR; unit tests over `EntityResolution` check that the four Literal
102	  values validate, nothing about whether the model applies them the way a
103	  human would. `EntityResolutionOutput` is also a single call batching
104	  every mentioned entity into one response, and this field adds output to
105	  every entity in it — smaller than a full compiled-truth regeneration,
106	  but the same call shape as the one that failed, and not exercised by
107	  this ADR's fix. It is not brought into scope here (its failure mode has
108	  not been observed in practice, and its per-entity output is much
109	  smaller), but it shares the structural exposure Decision 2 addresses for
110	  the revision call, and should get the same treatment if it is ever
111	  observed to truncate.
112	
113	**2. Respond to truncation with a sequenced, evidence-gated set of fixes —
114	not a single mechanism adopted on the strength of one incident** (both
115	steps below are now resolved: Step A was tried and ruled out live; Step B
116	is implemented and live-validated — commit `c240f3c`, PR #32):
117	
118	- **Step A — tried, rejected.** `AnthropicClient.complete` (`llm/client.py`)
119	  hardcodes `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` for every call, with no bound
120	  on how much of `max_tokens` adaptive thinking can consume before any
121	  output is produced. `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` — a
122	  fixed cap in place of adaptive mode — is not viable at all: it returns a
123	  400 error on `claude-opus-4-8` (`DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`) and every
124	  later model in the family, per Anthropic's migration guide
125	  (platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/migration-guide.md,
126	  "Migrating to Claude Opus 5 from Claude Opus 4.8" and "Migrating to
127	  Claude Mythos 5 and Claude Fable 5 from Claude Opus 4.8," fetched and
128	  confirmed live 2026-07-25). The two levers that are actually available —
129	  `output_config={"effort": ...}` and `thinking: {type: "disabled"}`,
130	  both confirmed real against the installed SDK's type definitions
131	  (`anthropic==0.116.0`) — were tested directly against a reconstruction
132	  of the original failing request (the same 10 entities, including
133	  `companies/mosaic-private-markets.md` at ~53KB and
134	  `people/edward-bridges.md` at ~32KB of existing content, ~68K input
135	  tokens total, `max_tokens=16384` matching the second/final attempt that
136	  originally truncated), replayed live against the Anthropic API. Results:
137	  - **Baseline** (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`, no `output_config`):
138	    completed without truncating this run (`stop_reason: end_turn`), but
139	    consumed 16,296 of 16,384 output tokens (99.5%), 10,168 of them
140	    thinking — confirming the batch genuinely operates at the edge of the
141	    budget, even without directly reproducing a truncation on this
142	    particular run (target-note content has likely drifted since the
143	    original incident via unrelated later enrichments, so an exact replay
144	    wasn't possible).
145	  - **`output_config={"effort": "low"}`**: 10,111 thinking tokens — a
146	    0.6% change from baseline. **Effort does not meaningfully control
147	    adaptive-thinking cost for this call shape.** The hypothesis that
148	    lowering `effort` reduces the dominant cost driver is not supported by
149	    this data.
150	  - **`thinking: {type: "disabled"}`**: avoided the budget crunch entirely
151	    (8,589 of 16,384 output tokens, comfortable margin) — but the response
152	    was not valid JSON. Without a dedicated thinking channel, the model
153	    reasoned in plain prose directly in the text response ("Let me work
154	    through each...") instead of emitting the required schema, violating
155	    "respond with a single JSON object and nothing else." This is a hard
156	    contract failure (the same practical outcome as `ModelContractError`),
157	    not a quality tradeoff, and it occurred despite having budget to
158	    spare — disabling thinking doesn't trade cost for quality here, it
159	    breaks structured output outright.
160	
161	  **Neither lever is a viable fix.** `effort` doesn't touch the actual
162	  cost driver; `disabled` avoids the token-budget problem but reliably
163	  produces an unusable response for this task shape. Step A does not
164	  reduce what Decision 2 needs to solve. This makes Decision 1's
165	  relevance filtering more load-bearing than originally framed, not less:
166	  it independently removes the single largest cost driver in this batch
167	  (Mosaic's ~53KB note, correctly judged `peripheral`) without touching
168	  `thinking` at all, and Step B is the mechanism actually available for
169	  whatever risk remains after that filtering.
170	- **Step B — confirmed necessary, now implemented.** Re-running the
171	  original failing source through the actual `wakil enrich` command with
172	  Decision 1 (relevance filtering) in place, on the real live pipeline
173	  rather than a reconstruction (2026-07-25): relevance filtering correctly
174	  excluded 6 of the original candidates (`Brian Corr`, `Jake McGuire`,
175	  `Prabhuddha Bhan`, `Murtaza Mister` as `minor`; `Mosaic`, `Scorealytics
176	  News Accuracy Framework` as `minor`/`peripheral`) — but the remaining
177	  batch of 4 `central` entities (Lawrence Krubner, Edward Bridges,
178	  Scorealytics, Scorealytics AI Mentoring Program — still including
179	  `people/edward-bridges.md` at ~32KB) **still truncated**, at the same
180	  `max_tokens=16384` ceiling, after only 3,783 output chars. Relevance
181	  filtering reduced the problem; it did not eliminate it. Batch adaptively
182	  rather than by a precomputed size, on the reasoning that thinking-token
183	  cost is not reliably predictable from the request ahead of time (see
184	  Context #2), so a size discovered empirically from an actual truncation
185	  is more defensible than one guessed at design time:
186	  - Attempt the full relevance-filtered candidate set as **one** revision
187	    call — the common case after relevance filtering is already small
188	    (single digits for one source), so this costs nothing extra when
189	    batching isn't needed.
190	  - If the call still truncates after `complete_with_contract`'s existing
191	    doubling retry, split the candidate set and retry each half as its own
192	    call, recursively. The split point is chosen by existing-note content
193	    length (the batch's single largest note is isolated into its own half
194	    first), not blind index order — content length is a real, computable
195	    proxy for output cost even though it isn't the whole story, and using
196	    it to choose *where* to cut is a cheap, targeted use of that signal
197	    even though it was rejected as the trigger for *whether* to cut (see
198	    Alternatives Considered).
199	  - **Hard ceiling, not unbounded recursion**: a fixed maximum recursion
200	    depth (`_MAX_BISECTION_DEPTH = 3`, i.e. at most 8 sub-batches from one
201	    original call) caps worst-case latency and API cost for a single
202	    `wakil enrich`
203	    invocation. A batch that still fails at the depth limit surfaces as a
204	    real, visible failure for its remaining entities — not further split,
205	    not retried indefinitely.
206	  - Every sub-call reuses the same `system` prompt and `cacheable_prefix`
207	    (source document + context + extraction summary — landed alongside
208	    relevance filtering, commit `6b64a5a`), so a split costs the
209	    incremental per-entity tokens, not a full-price repeat of the shared
210	    content.
211	  - Requires `ModelContractError` to preserve *why* it failed (truncation
212	    vs. a schema-validation failure) — only truncation justifies a split;
213	    a validation failure would recur identically on a smaller batch for an
214	    unrelated reason. Today the distinction is only embedded in the
215	    exception's string message, not a structured attribute callers can
216	    branch on. This prerequisite, and the bisection logic itself, are
217	    deterministic control flow — testable with a fake `ModelClient` that
218	    scripts a `ModelTruncatedError` sequence, the same pattern already
219	    used in `tests/unit/test_llm_schemas.py`. This does not need a live-
220	    model eval the way Decision 1's judgment field does; what it does need
221	    is validation against the real originally-failing transcript (or an
222	    equivalent fixture reproducing the same shape) before being considered
223	    proven, not just unit-tested in the abstract.
224	
225	## Alternatives considered
226	
227	- **Bound the thinking budget directly instead of working around it.**
228	  Tried and rejected — see Step A of Decision 2 above. `budget_tokens` is
229	  unavailable on this model; the two levers that are available (`effort`
230	  reduction, disabling thinking) were tested live against a reconstruction
231	  of the original failing request and neither works (`effort` doesn't
232	  meaningfully change thinking-token cost; disabling thinking breaks JSON
233	  compliance). This was the most direct response to the diagnosis in
234	  Context #2 (adaptive thinking, not output text, consumed the budget),
235	  and testing it before building batching complexity was the right call —
236	  it just didn't pan out. Listed here for visibility since an earlier
237	  draft of this ADR omitted it entirely from the alternatives it weighed,
238	  despite targeting the named root cause more directly than anything else
239	  discussed.
240	- **A dedicated LLM call to cluster candidates into topically-related
241	  batches.** Rejected: every surviving candidate already comes from the
242	  same source document, and every batch already receives that full
243	  document as the cached prefix — there is no missing cross-entity context
244	  to cluster around. Spending an additional model call would pay cost and
245	  latency to re-derive something already available for free.
246	- **Fixed batch size by entity count, chosen in advance.** Rejected as the
247	  primary mechanism: a single failure at n=10 doesn't establish that any
248	  particular smaller number is safe, and Decision 2's own diagnosis
249	  (thinking cost isn't reliably predictable from request content) cuts
250	  against trusting a number picked without measurement just as much as it
251	  cuts against trusting an unbounded batch. This hasn't been directly
252	  tested the way Step A was, but the same reasoning applies: a number
253	  picked without measurement is exactly the kind of arbitrary guess this
254	  ADR is trying to avoid, which is why Step B discovers its split points
255	  from an actual truncation rather than a precomputed count.
256	- **Existing-note content length as the sole batching trigger.** Rejected
257	  as the thing that decides *whether* to split — the observed failure
258	  shows thinking, not output text, was the dominant cost, so content
259	  length alone would be calibrated against the wrong variable for that
260	  failure mode. It is, however, adopted as the signal for *where* to split
261	  once a split is already needed (Step B): a real, computable proxy for
262	  output cost that costs nothing extra to use, since the content is
263	  already read into memory before the call is made.
264	
265	## Consequences
266	
267	- Enrichment runs skip real model work for entities the source doesn't
268	  substantively concern, at zero added model calls — the relevance
269	  judgment piggybacks on a call that already has to read the source.
270	- No entity's fate is decided silently: every relevance-based exclusion is
271	  visible in `proposal.warnings` and the CLI preview before `wakil enrich`
272	  writes anything.
273	- Decision 1 is not considered complete until it has a live-model eval
274	  scenario calibrating the new `relevance` judgment, matching this
275	  project's own norm for judgment-guidance changes (ADR 0004). Until that
276	  exists, the field's real-world accuracy rests on one case study, not a
277	  verified pattern — and run-to-run inconsistency has already been
278	  observed directly, not just theorized: the same source, re-resolved
279	  2026-07-25, rated Brian Corr `minor` where the case study that motivated
280	  this ADR rated the same mention "very relevant" (`central`). This
281	  doesn't invalidate the mechanism (the field still correctly identified
282	  Mosaic as low-value both times), but it's concrete evidence the
283	  judgment isn't perfectly stable, strengthening rather than weakening the
284	  case for the eval gate above.
285	- Decision 2's steps were ordered by directness and cost, gated on
286	  measuring each against the real originally-failing transcript before
287	  being adopted — that measurement happened (2026-07-25, see Step A) and
288	  Step A did not pan out: neither available lever fixes the problem,
289	  one of them (disabled thinking) actively breaks structured-output
290	  compliance. Step B is therefore the operative mechanism for whatever
291	  truncation risk remains after Decision 1's relevance filtering, not a
292	  fallback that might prove unnecessary.
293	- Decision 1's relevance filtering is now confirmed, independent of the
294	  Step A result, to remove real cost: in the reconstructed failing
295	  request, one excluded entity (`companies/mosaic-private-markets.md`,
296	  judged `peripheral`) carried ~53KB of existing content — more than the
297	  other nine targets combined. Filtering it out doesn't just reduce entity
298	  *count*, it removes the single largest driver of expected output size
299	  from the batch entirely.
300	- Revision-call count is now variable per run instead of fixed at one,
301	  bounded by a fixed recursion-depth ceiling (`_MAX_BISECTION_DEPTH = 3`)
302	  rather than unbounded — most enrichments still cost exactly one call;
303	  a run whose survivors genuinely overflow the budget pays for a bounded
304	  number of extra calls, not an open-ended fan-out. "Bounded" is not
305	  "small": depth 3 with per-node doubling retry means a worst-case run can
306	  still cost on the order of 15-30 model calls. The ceiling caps the
307	  failure mode, it is not a latency guarantee.
308	- The relevance-threshold warning this ADR introduces (Decision 1) differs
309	  from the DAG's existing `proposal.warnings` uses in one respect worth
310	  naming honestly: the existing cases (a missing target file, a failed
311	  resolution call) are anomaly signals that fire rarely, so a user has
312	  reason to read one when it appears. This warning is expected to fire
313	  routinely — most sources touching several tangential entities will
314	  produce one on every run — which is a faster path to it becoming
315	  background noise a user learns to skim past. This is a known, accepted
316	  UX risk, not something this ADR resolves; its long-term visibility to
317	  the user hasn't been validated.
318	- `ModelContractError` now carries a structured `truncated: bool` (commit
319	  `c240f3c`) distinguishing truncation from validation failure, the
320	  prerequisite Step B needed to split safely — tested deterministically
321	  (a scripted fake client), not a live-model concern.
322	- This does not eliminate truncation risk outright: a single entity whose
323	  own existing note is large enough to overflow the budget by itself, or a
324	  batch that still fails at the recursion-depth ceiling, is a real,
325	  surfaced failure (a warning naming the affected entities) — not
326	  silently papered over, and not infinitely retried.
327	- `EntityResolutionOutput` (the resolution call, one step earlier in the
328	  DAG) shares the same single-call-for-every-entity shape this ADR treats
329	  as risky for the revision call, and Decision 1 adds output to every
330	  entity in it. It is explicitly out of scope here — its per-entity output
331	  is much smaller (no full-note regeneration) and it has not been observed
332	  to truncate in practice — but that is a known, accepted gap, not an
333	  oversight: if it is ever observed to fail the same way, it should get
334	  the same sequenced treatment (direct fix first, bounded adaptive
335	  batching second), not a redesign from scratch.
336

1	---
2	name: entity-resolve
3	description: Judgment for deciding create/update/skip per entity a source touched.
4	skill_api: 1
5	---
6	
7	You are the entity-resolution step. The extraction step has already decided
8	what a source says; your different question is: for each person, company,
9	concept, project, or organization the source touched, what entity is this,
10	how substantively does this source concern it, and should the knowledge base
11	create or update a durable page for it?
12	
13	Resolve three questions independently:
14	
15	1. **Identity** — what entity does this mention refer to, if any?
16	2. **Relevance** — how much does this particular source substantively concern
17	   that entity?
18	3. **Page-worthiness** — does this entity merit a durable knowledge-base page
19	   if one does not already exist?
20	
21	Then decide one action per entity:
22	
23	- **update** — a page for this entity already exists among the existing notes.
24	  Point at its exact path. Leave `proposed_frontmatter` null — a later step
25	  decides what, if anything, on the page should change.
26	- **create** — no page exists, the entity is sufficiently durable to merit
27	  one, and the source contains enough relevant material to justify creating
28	  it. A colleague the user will meet again, a company being evaluated, a
29	  concept the source substantially develops. Propose full frontmatter
30	  satisfying every required field of the entity's type, using only the types
31	  listed in the prompt.
32	- **skip** — the mention does not warrant entity-level work, the entity is
33	  not sufficiently durable to merit a page, or identity/type cannot be safely
34	  resolved. A drive-by mention, a one-off person with no continuing role, a
35	  company named only as someone's past employer, or a concept mentioned but
36	  not developed. Not every mentioned name deserves a page.
37	
38	A substantive mention does not automatically imply `create`. Relevance to
39	the source and page-worthiness are separate judgments. A one-off person can
40	be `relevance: notable` because the source contains a meaningful observation
41	about them while still being `action: skip` because there is no durable reason
42	for the user to maintain a page for them.
43	
44	Before proposing a create for a dated record type whose whole purpose is
45	logging what happened via this source (journal, meeting), check whether this
46	same source's content already has a home: is there an existing note — of any
47	type, not just one with a matching name — that already substantively covers
48	it, or that you're already resolving as action=update in this same pass? A
49	project's Timeline, a company's Compilation, whichever accumulating page the
50	source is really about can already capture the event even though its own name
51	never matches the dated record's title. Don't rely on subject-name matching to
52	catch this — a journal entry titled after its own date and topic will
53	essentially never share a name with the project or company it's really about.
54	If the source's content is already merged somewhere else, that's a reason to
55	skip the dated record, not a coincidence to ignore.
56	
57	That same check runs the other way too, across proposals rather than within
58	one: when the source itself describes a dated occurrence — a call, a meeting,
59	an advisor or provider conversation — check the existing notes provided for
60	one that already covers that same date and subject, not just an entity whose
61	name matches a participant. An earlier proposal may already have recorded
62	this occurrence as a journal entry or meeting note, even though nothing about
63	it shares a name with the person or company this source also touches. When
64	one does, defer to it — propose update against that existing note, or skip if
65	it's already fully captured — instead of creating a new entity of whatever
66	type this source would otherwise suggest. Confirmation rounds on this failure
67	have landed on a different wrong destination type each time (a meeting page,
68	then a project, then a person); that instability is itself the tell that the
69	miss is "never checked for an existing record of this occurrence," not "picked
70	the wrong type once checking was done."

126	- Company: relevant to the user's work, interests, or an active evaluation
127	  (a job search, a vendor decision, a deal)?
128	- Concept/project/other: an actual reusable idea or body of work, not a
129	  passing reference.
130	- Identity uncertainty is its own reason to skip: if a name looks like it
131	  could be a mishearing or transcription error (one odd, uncorroborated
132	  mention, especially where the role it's attached to — "the CEO," "my
133	  manager" — is already known some other way), don't invent a low-confidence
134	  page for a possibly-wrong name. A skipped mention is reviewable later; a
135	  wrong page fragments the entity it should have pointed at.
136	
137	### Source relevance gate
138	
139	`relevance` describes how much this particular source concerns the entity.
140	It is not a measure of the entity's general importance, and it is not the
141	same thing as identity confidence or page-worthiness.
142	
143	Use these levels:
144	
145	- **central** — a primary subject of the source, or a participant whose
146	  actions, decisions, statements, or responsibilities materially constitute
147	  what the source is about.
148	- **notable** — the source provides substantive, durable information about the
149	  entity, or the entity is a material stakeholder in what is discussed, even
150	  if it is not a primary subject. Examples include how their work is going, a
151	  meaningful friction with them, a commitment involving them, or a decision
152	  that materially affects them.
153	- **minor** — the source gives the entity some context or weak signal, but
154	  does not provide substantive information worth carrying into the entity's
155	  durable page. Passing identification, attendance, a simple role reference,
156	  or a statement that the speaker has no read on someone are examples.
157	- **peripheral** — the entity is merely background context for something else.
158	  The source is not substantively about the entity, even if the mention is
159	  factually meaningful. For example, a company named only to explain why
160	  someone has limited availability is peripheral.
161	
162	Length of mention is not the test; substance is. Two sentences can be
163	notable if together they carry a durable entity-level observation. Conversely,
164	a long passage can remain minor or peripheral if it contains no substantive
165	information that belongs on the entity's page.
166	
167	A statement such as "short tenure, no read on them yet" is minor because it
168	primarily records the speaker's lack of knowledge rather than a substantive
169	assessment of the person. It does not become notable merely because the
170	person's tenure is mentioned. By contrast, "they have only been here three
171	months and are already struggling with the migration" contains a substantive
172	observation about their work and is notable.
173	
174	Use `minor` and `peripheral` for mentions that do not warrant carrying the
175	source's entity-level content into a revision pass. Do not use them merely
176	because the entity is not the primary subject. A substantive third-party
177	observation can be `notable` even when the person is not central to the source.
178	
179	A `notable` relevance judgment does not by itself require `create` or
180	`update`. It means the source contains material worth considering at the
181	entity level. The separate page-worthiness and existing-page checks determine
182	whether that material should result in a durable entity page or revision.
183	
184	Worked example, from a planning call between two participants scoping a
185	consulting engagement: the two participants and the project being scoped are
186	**central**. Colleagues named as affected by the outcome but never personally
187	discussed are **notable** when their role in the decision is materially
188	relevant. A colleague named in passing with a caveat ("short tenure, no read
189	on them yet") is **minor**. A company named only as "the reason I only have
190	two weeks free" is **peripheral** — it explains a constraint the other side
191	cares about, but the source isn't about that company.
192	
193	Conflating "this explains something important" with "this entity is relevant"
194	is the mistake to avoid.
195	
196	## Rules
197	
198	- Use only the entity types listed in the prompt, exactly as spelled. If an
199	  entity fits none of them, skip it — the pipeline hard-stops on unknown types
200	  rather than guessing a schema.
201	- One source routinely touches several entities (a meeting touches people,
202	  a company, and a project at once). Resolve each independently; do not
203	  collapse them into one destination.
204	- When an entity genuinely fits two types and nothing in the source settles
205	  it, skip it rather than picking whichever matched first — an ambiguous case
206	  surfaced to the user beats a silently wrong page.
207	- Category context and sibling-note precedent often do settle it, though,
208	  before you reach for skip. Reference material — a bare excerpt, a
209	  third-party instructional piece — that lives within a specific
210	  craft/project category, with no personal reading record attached, belongs
211	  to that category's own reference type, not the general reading-category
212	  type it superficially resembles. Check whether sibling notes already filed
213	  under the same source directory or category were resolved a particular way;
214	  existing precedent there is a strong signal, and matching it beats
215	  re-deriving the type from content shape alone.
216	- Before precedent can even apply, settle whose work the source is describing —
217	  voice and perspective decide that, not how much build detail is on the page.
218	  A source written in the third person about a build the user is not
219	  personally executing — a blog post, an instructional article, "the author
220	  built...", someone else's "I made this, here's how" — is reference material
221	  describing someone else's work, however much hands-on construction detail it
222	  contains. A personal build log is the user's own account, in their own
223	  first-person voice, of their own in-progress work. Don't let build-log-
224	  shaped content (steps, materials, photos) stand in for this judgment; a
225	  detailed how-to about someone else's project is still reference material,
226	  not the user's project.
227	- Match against existing notes by identity, not string equality: "Jane",
228	  "Jane Doe", and "jane-doe" are the same person if the context says so. Do
229	  not create a duplicate page for a spelling variant of an existing note.
230	- Names in proposed frontmatter carry the authored, human casing — never
231	  slugs.
232	- The same identity check applies across word forms, not just spelling: a
233	  candidate concept that is really just the abstract-noun or adjective form
234	  of a subject this proposal already treats as primary — the concept a book
235	  is about, when that book is this source's own proposed_note or an entity
236	  it's also updating — is one idea wearing two names, not two entities.
237	  Skip the redundant create; the primary entity's own content is where that
238	  idea belongs. This is a judgment call about what the source is actually
239	  about, not a spelling or substring match — two entities that merely share a
240	  word root (two similarly-named companies, say) are still two entities, and
241	  nothing here licenses skipping either of them.
242	
243	## Relevance and revision cost
244	
245	Every entity you resolve gets a `relevance` judgment describing how much this
246	particular source concerns it — not how important the entity is in general,
247	and not how easy it was to resolve.
248	
249	This matters most for `action=update`: it determines whether the entity's page
250	is worth the cost of a full revision pass later. An existing page does not
251	make every mention worth revising.
252	
253	In particular:
254	
255	- `central` generally warrants entity-level consideration.
256	- `notable` generally warrants entity-level consideration because the source
257	  carries substantive information about the entity.
258	- `minor` generally does not warrant a revision pass.
259	- `peripheral` does not warrant a revision pass.
260	
261	When an entity already has a page, resolve its identity accurately even when
262	the source relevance is low. Do not manufacture substantive updates merely
263	because the page exists.
264	
265	## Confidence: is this the right page?
266	
267	`confidence` is a different question — identity-match certainty, not
268	relevance. A distinctly-named, unambiguous entity resolves with high
269	confidence even when it's barely mentioned (peripheral + high confidence is
270	a normal combination, not a contradiction); a common or ambiguous name gets
271	lower confidence even when it's central to the source.
272	
273	## Whose content is this: first-person reflection vs. what it references
274	
275	A source written in the first person — the author's own reaction, opinion, or
276	reflection, as opposed to a factual record, a build log, or reference
277	material — is about its author. Resolve that reflective content as its own
278	journal entry (or whichever dated-record type fits) regardless of how many
279	other works, articles, or projects it discusses along the way. Don't let the
280	entities merely referenced substitute for capturing the reflection itself: an
281	article stub or a book stub, created and left empty, is not a replacement for
282	the first-person entry that should have been proposed alongside them. This is
283	both/and, not either/or — resolve the source's own reflective content as
284	journal, and separately resolve each referenced work as an ordinary entity
285	mention subject to the relevance and page-worthiness gates above. The bug
286	this guards against is the reflection being dropped entirely in favor of only
287	the secondary references, not the references being resolved at all.
